html:
Apartheid, Afrikaans for "separateness", was the system of racial segregation written into law in South Africa from 1948 to 1994, and also imposed in South West Africa, now Namibia. It kept political and economic power in the hands of the white minority.

Segregation was older: a law of 1913 already kept most land for whites, and the gold mines ran on controlled black migrant labour. But the National Party won the 1948 election promising apartheid, and built it into a full legal system:

  • every person was classified by race as White, Coloured, Indian or Black;
  • separate areas for each group, with millions forcibly moved from their homes;
  • pass laws that controlled where black people could live and work;
  • "homelands" for black people, some declared independent so that their people lost South African citizenship;
  • separate and unequal schools, and bans on mixed marriage.

Resistance grew. The African National Congress adopted the Freedom Charter in 1955. Police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, after which the ANC was banned and turned to armed struggle. Its leader Nelson Mandela was jailed for life in 1964. Students rose in the Soweto uprising of 1976.

In the 1980s township revolts, strikes, foreign sanctions and sports boycotts put the state under heavy pressure. In 1990 President F. W. de Klerk lifted the bans and freed Mandela. Talks led to the first election open to all races in April 1994, which ended apartheid.
